Questions, plainly answered

Understand the flow.Then try it.

What runs, where AI helps and what an engineer still needs to review.

The framework

Is an LLM doing every step?

The configured flow runs routine steps as code and engineering-tool calls. An LLM helps prepare or adapt that flow, rather than being asked to choose every action during each normal run. AI-assisted circuit creation, customisation or error diagnosis can still consume tokens.

How is this different from an agent handling the whole job?

The emphasis is on turning engineering know-how into a reusable framework: explicit steps, constraints, tool connections and acceptance checks. AI helps establish or change that structure. The routine job then follows it, giving engineers a clearer execution trail to review.

How do expert circuits and layouts help?

A curated library of circuit and expert-reviewed layout pairs is a proposed way to guide and test framework extensions. Using examples as context is different from training model weights. The dataset, permissions and exact training or retrieval method still need to be defined.

Getting started

What can I try today?

Open the cloud layout tool and begin with a supported catalogue circuit. Explore the available floorplan and layout controls, then inspect the physical-check results. The recording on this page shows examples of that process.

Can I use my own circuit or PDK?

A netlist must use supported devices and a compatible process setup. Check the current support in the cloud tool before starting. Assisted adaptation to another PDK is a planned service; device, extraction and checking support must be agreed for each process.

Does this replace the layout engineer?

No. The engineer defines what the circuit must do, sets constraints and reviews the result. The aim is to reduce repetitive implementation work while preserving engineering judgement and final approval.

Is digital verification available on this page?

The current public demonstration focuses on analog layout and physical checks. Digital design and verification are part of the wider flow the team is developing; they are not a completed public service demonstrated here.

Checks and data

What do DRC and LVS actually prove?

Design-rule checking (DRC) tests geometry against the selected rules. Layout-versus-schematic checking (LVS) compares connectivity with the source circuit. Electrical performance, reliability and project sign-off require the applicable additional tests and expert review.

What happens after a change or an unexpected failure?

A changed layout needs renewed checks for the affected requirements before acceptance. Unexpected failures can need agent-assisted diagnosis or specialist attention. Any repair must be reviewed and the relevant evidence refreshed; a successful old run is not approval of a new design.

What happens to designs I upload?

This landing page does not collect or store netlists. The cloud tool is a separate service, so confirm its storage, access and retention arrangements before using confidential work. Private project workspaces and permission-based contribution of examples are planned capabilities. Any future reuse of designs for training would require separate explicit permission.

Value and evaluation

Where should the savings come from?

The target is specialist time spent on implementation, revisions and checking, alongside setup and EDA-tool costs where suitable open-source tools can be used. The wider programme also targets digital design and verification. The opportunity depends on the actual project and its requirements.

How will you demonstrate a cost or time saving?

Compare the same scope, circuit requirements and acceptance criteria. Count hands-on engineering time, elapsed time, tool and compute costs, rework and review effort. Recorded layout-generation time is one measurement; it does not establish a whole-project saving. A project-level cost breakdown is being prepared.

Can trial feedback improve the platform?

Yes, feedback can help identify useful constraints, awkward steps and remaining manual work. The guided trial lets you download your own notes. A shared submission or challenge system is a future step, with clear access controls and permission for any contributed circuit or layout data.
